title: Neck haematoma after thyroid surgery
subtitle: SCOOP at the bedside, then theatre

sources.org: Difficult Airway Society (DAS), British Association of Endocrine and Thyroid Surgeons (BAETS) and ENT UK
sources.title: Management of haematoma after thyroid surgery: systematic review and multidisciplinary consensus guidelines (Iliff HA, El-Boghdadly K, Ahmad I et al., Anaesthesia)
Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults (Frerk C et al., Br J Anaesth)
American Thyroid Association statement on outpatient thyroidectomy (Terris DJ et al., Thyroid)

red_flags.text: DESATS: Difficulty swallowing or discomfort, Early warning score change, Swelling, Anxiety, Tachypnoea or difficulty breathing, Stridor.
Stridor or a rapidly enlarging neck: airway compromise is imminent. Venous congestion and laryngeal oedema, not just tracheal compression, close the airway.
Desaturation is a late sign. Do not wait for it.
Most haematomas present within the first hours after surgery, but late presentations occur, including after discharge.

do_now.text: Call for help immediately: senior surgeon, senior anaesthetist, and the emergency team. Sit the patient up and give high-flow oxygen.
If the airway is compromised, open the wound at the bedside without waiting for theatre: SCOOP. Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack.
Open all layers including the strap muscle closure, and evacuate the clot with a gloved finger; then pack loosely with a gauze swab.
Keep a haematoma kit at the bedside of every post-thyroidectomy patient: suture or clip remover, scalpel, gauze and gloves.

assess.text: Regular structured neck checks in recovery and on the ward by staff trained to recognise DESATS and to perform SCOOP.
Measure the progression: neck circumference markings or serial photographs help staff see change.
Airway assessment by the anaesthetist even after decompression: laryngeal oedema persists after the clot is removed.

investigate.text: No imaging for a suspected expanding haematoma with airway symptoms. Imaging delays the treatment.
FBC, coagulation and crossmatch once the airway is safe.
Review antithrombotic drugs and any peri-operative anticoagulation.

resuscitate.text: After SCOOP, continue oxygen, keep the patient sitting up, and transfer to theatre for formal exploration and haemostasis.
Plan tracheal intubation for an experienced anaesthetist with difficult airway equipment; evacuate the haematoma before induction whenever possible, as this often improves the view.
Be prepared for front-of-neck access, knowing that the anatomy is distorted by oedema and blood.

definitive.text: Formal re-exploration in theatre: evacuate clot, irrigate, identify and control the bleeding point, check both recurrent laryngeal nerves and the parathyroids, and close.
Correct coagulopathy and review the restart of antithrombotic drugs explicitly.
Day-case or short-stay thyroidectomy only with a protocol for observation, a haematoma kit and clear advice for the patient to return immediately.

escalate.text: Senior anaesthetist and senior surgeon at once for any suspected haematoma. This is a team emergency.
Critical care after re-intubation for laryngeal oedema, or after a difficult airway.
Report and debrief every haematoma; review whether recognition and SCOOP training worked.

notes: Opening the wound feels drastic on a ward. It is the single action that saves the airway, and the wound heals well afterwards.
Removing only skin sutures is not enough; the strap muscle layer contains the haematoma and must be opened too.
Laryngeal oedema from venous congestion explains why intubation is still difficult after the clot is out.
